changes.correctAnswer: Administer alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 hours
changes.explanation:
Persistent hypotension from PE is AHA/ACC PE Category E (high risk). With no contraindication, reperfusion with systemic thrombolysis plus anticoagulation reduces death; alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 hours is the labeled regimen.

Why others are wrong:
• Enoxaparin alone: LMWH is preferred for stable PE, but anticoagulation alone does not relieve obstruction in shock.
• Apixaban: oral agents are for stable patients after initial treatment.
• IVC filter: only for those who cannot be anticoagulated; it does not restore perfusion.
• D-dimer: PE is already confirmed on CTPA.

Takeaway: PE with persistent hypotension needs reperfusion now (systemic thrombolysis, or catheter/surgical therapy if lytics are contraindicated) on top of anticoagulation.

blindSolve.reason: Confirmed PE with BP 78/50 despite fluids = high-risk/obstructive shock; no bleeding contraindication, so reperfusion. B/C are anticoagulation only, D for anticoagulation contraindication, E unnecessary after CTPA.

changes.correctAnswer: Perform emergent coronary angiography with primary PCI
changes.explanation:
This is an inferior STEMI at a PCI-capable center. Primary PCI is the preferred reperfusion strategy, with a first-medical-contact-to-device goal of 90 minutes or less, and the ECG alone is enough to activate the cath lab.

Why others are wrong:
• Serial troponin: biomarkers are not needed to diagnose STEMI, and waiting delays reperfusion.
• Echocardiogram: may help later but should not delay the cath lab.
• Tenecteplase: fibrinolysis is for when timely PCI is not available.
• CT angiography: equal arm BPs and pulses make aortic dissection unlikely; imaging would delay reperfusion.

Takeaway: ST elevation in two contiguous leads with ischemic symptoms means immediate reperfusion. Do not wait for troponin.

items.guideline: 2025 ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI Guideline for the Management of Patients With Acute Coronary Syndromes (PPCI preferred; FMC-to-device <=90 min)

blindSolve.reason: Diagnostic inferior STEMI on ECG with ongoing symptoms at a PCI-capable hospital needs immediate primary PCI; troponin/echo/CT delay reperfusion, lytics are second-line when PCI is available.

changes.explanation:
Syncope during exertion, a family history of sudden death, a murmur that gets louder with lower preload, and LVH with deep narrow Q waves all point to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. TTE is the recommended first imaging test for suspected HCM. She should be held out of sports until cardiology evaluates her.

Why others are wrong:
• Iron: mild microcytic anemia does not explain exertional syncope or the murmur. Treating it first delays a diagnosis that can kill.
• Tilt-table: for suspected reflex syncope, which happens with prodrome, not during exertion.
• EEG: nothing suggests a seizure.
• Return to sports: unsafe until HCM is excluded.

Takeaway: syncope during exertion is cardiac until proven otherwise. Get an ECG and echocardiogram.

items.guideline: 2024 AHA/ACC/AMSSM/HRS/PACES/SCMR Guideline for the Management of Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (TTE recommended in initial evaluation of suspected HCM); 2017 ACC/AHA/HRS Syncope Guideline (exertional syncope = high-risk feature)

blindSolve.reason: Exertional syncope without prodrome, sudden-death family history, dynamic murmur louder with Valsalva/standing, LVH with Q waves = HCM; echo next. Anemia is mild and incidental; tilt/EEG/clearance wrong.

changes.scenario: A 50-year-old man with type 2 diabetes treated with metformin (eGFR 85 mL/min/1.73 m2) presents with 3 days of a painful swelling on his left thigh. Examination shows a 4-cm tender, fluctuant mass with 3 cm of surrounding erythema and warmth. Temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F), HR 98/min, BP 132/80 mm Hg, and RR 16/min. He has no drug allergies.
changes.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
changes.options: {"options": ["Cephalexin 500 mg orally four times daily alone", "Incision and drainage plus trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 1 double-strength tablet (160/800 mg) orally twice daily", "Incision and drainage plus cephalexin 500 mg orally four times daily", "Hospital admission for IV vancomycin without drainage", "Warm compresses and recheck in 48 hours"], "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "cellulitis", "blueprintSystem": "dermatologic", "generationMeta": {"batchId": "pance-2026-06-27-7e5roo", "slotIndex": 3, "model": "gpt-4o-mini", "pipelineVersion": "gpt-4o-mini-pance-v1", "blueprintAligned": true, "difficultyRating": 2, "qcScore": 9, "generatedAt": "2026-06-27T21:03:02.626Z", "qcFlags": []}}
changes.correctAnswer: Incision and drainage plus trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 1 double-strength tablet (160/800 mg) orally twice daily
changes.explanation:
A fluctuant mass is an abscess, a purulent SSTI. Fever above 38°C with HR above 90 meets SIRS criteria, making this a moderate purulent infection. IDSA recommends incision and drainage plus empiric MRSA-active oral therapy such as TMP-SMX (1 to 2 DS tablets twice daily) or doxycycline.

Why others are wrong:
• Cephalexin alone: no source control and no MRSA coverage. Cephalexin targets streptococci in nonpurulent cellulitis.
• I&D plus cephalexin: source control is right, but the antibiotic misses community-acquired MRSA.
• IV vancomycin without drainage: an abscess needs drainage, and he is not severely ill.
• Warm compresses: undertreats a febrile patient with a drainable abscess.

Takeaway: drain purulent infections. Add MRSA-active antibiotics when systemic signs or risk factors are present.

items.guideline: IDSA 2014 Practice Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Management of Skin and Soft Tissue Infections (purulent SSTI algorithm: moderate = I&D + empiric TMP-SMX or doxycycline; TMP-SMX 1-2 DS tabs bid)

blindSolve.reason: Fluctuant 4 cm = abscess needing I&D; fever 38.4 + HR 98 = SIRS so add antibiotic; purulent infection → MRSA coverage, so TMP-SMX over cephalexin. Normal eGFR, no allergy, so TMP-SMX safe.

changes.scenario: A 10-year-old girl (32 kg) is brought to the emergency department with 2 days of severe right ear pain and a temperature of 39.3°C (102.7°F). The right tympanic membrane is erythematous, bulging, and immobile, and tympanometry is flat (type B). She had three episodes of acute otitis media over the past 2 years, the most recent 8 months ago. She has taken no antibiotics in the past 30 days, has no drug allergies, and has no conjunctivitis or postauricular swelling.
changes.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
changes.options: {"options": ["High-dose amoxicillin 90 mg/kg/day orally in 2 divided doses plus ibuprofen for pain", "Ibuprofen alone with observation for 48 to 72 hours", "Tympanostomy tube placement", "CT of the temporal bones", "Ciprofloxacin-dexamethasone otic drops"], "taskCategory": "labs", "blueprintTopic": "otitis", "blueprintSystem": "eent", "generationMeta": {"batchId": "pance-2026-06-16-2tjksb", "slotIndex": 1, "model": "gpt-4o-mini", "pipelineVersion": "gpt-4o-mini-pance-v1", "blueprintAligned": true, "difficultyRating": 5, "qcScore": 9, "generatedAt": "2026-06-16T14:50:44.289Z", "qcFlags": []}}
changes.correctAnswer: High-dose amoxicillin 90 mg/kg/day orally in 2 divided doses plus ibuprofen for pain
changes.explanation:
A bulging TM with severe otalgia and fever of 39°C or higher is severe AOM. AAP recommends antibiotics rather than observation and analgesia for every child. First-line therapy is high-dose amoxicillin at 80 to 90 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses when there has been no amoxicillin in the past 30 days and no concurrent purulent conjunctivitis.

Why others are wrong:
• Observation: an option only for nonsevere AOM, not with high fever and severe pain.
• Tympanostomy tubes: an elective option for recurrent AOM (3 episodes in 6 months, or 4 in 12 months with 1 in the past 6). She does not meet this, and tubes do not treat an acute episode.
• CT: only if a complication such as mastoiditis is suspected.
• Otic drops: for otitis externa or tube otorrhea with an intact canal path, not AOM behind an intact TM.

Takeaway: treat severe AOM with high-dose amoxicillin plus analgesia.

items.guideline: AAP Clinical Practice Guideline: The Diagnosis and Management of Acute Otitis Media (Lieberthal et al., Pediatrics 2013)

blindSolve.reason: Bulging TM + fever 39.3 + severe pain = severe AOM → antibiotics, not observation; no recent amoxicillin/conjunctivitis → high-dose amoxicillin; 3 episodes/2 yr doesn't meet tube criteria; no complication for CT; drops don't treat AOM.

changes.correctAnswer: Measure total and direct (conjugated) serum bilirubin
changes.explanation:
Physiologic jaundice should be gone by 2 weeks in a formula-fed infant. AAP 2022 recommends measuring total and direct (or conjugated) bilirubin in formula-fed infants still jaundiced at 2 weeks, and breastfed infants at 3 to 4 weeks, to detect cholestasis such as biliary atresia. Outcomes in biliary atresia depend on early surgery.

Why others are wrong:
• Reassurance: persistent, worsening jaundice at 2 weeks is not physiologic and needs fractionation first.
• Soy formula: no evidence of milk-protein intolerance, and it does not address cholestasis.
• Phototherapy: 12 mg/dL is below treatment thresholds at this age, and phototherapy does nothing for conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.

Takeaway: jaundice at 2 weeks (formula-fed) or 3 to 4 weeks (breastfed) means total plus direct bilirubin.

blindSolve.reason: Formula-fed, still jaundiced and worsening at 2 weeks: must exclude cholestasis/biliary atresia by fractionating bilirubin before any reassurance; 12 is below phototherapy thresholds; soy irrelevant.

changes.explanation:
For adults, CDC defines BMI 25.0 to <30 as overweight, 30 to <35 as class 1 obesity, 35 to <40 as class 2, and 40 or higher as class 3. At 29.0 she is overweight. The history and exam give no reason to suspect hypothyroidism, Cushing syndrome, or binge eating disorder.

Why others are wrong:
• Normal weight: 18.5 to <25.
• Class 1 obesity: starts at 30.
• Class 2 obesity: 35 to <40.

Takeaway: classify adult weight by BMI cut points. A BMI of 25 to 29.9 is overweight, not obesity. With a family history of type 2 diabetes, this is a chance to counsel on lifestyle and consider diabetes screening.

changes.correctAnswer: Increase atorvastatin to 40 to 80 mg daily
changes.explanation:
Atorvastatin 10 mg is a moderate-intensity statin. For a primary-prevention adult at high (10% or greater) PREVENT risk, the 2026 ACC/AHA dyslipidemia guideline recommends a high-intensity statin, such as atorvastatin 40 to 80 mg, with an LDL-C goal below 70 mg/dL, alongside lifestyle therapy. Non-statin agents are added only if the goal is not reached on the maximally tolerated statin.

Why others are wrong:
• Ezetimibe now: skips statin intensification. Ezetimibe is the add-on after maximal tolerated statin therapy.
• Lifestyle alone: important as an adjunct but will not bring LDL-C from 160 to below 70.
• Pravastatin 40 mg: also moderate intensity, so no gain.

Takeaway: maximize statin intensity before adding non-statin therapy.
